title: Exact Solutions of the Dunkl--Pauli Equation in the Presence of a Magnetic Field from an su(1,1) Algebraic Approach
abstract: We investigate the two-dimensional Dunkl--Pauli equation for a spin--$1/2$ particle in the presence of an external magnetic field within an algebraic framework. While previous studies have provided exact solutions of the Dunkl--Pauli system, its underlying dynamical symmetry and algebraic structure remain largely unexplored. By employing Schrödinger factorization, we construct the generators of the $\mathfrak{su}(1,1)$ algebra and establish the associated symmetry of the radial sector. The energy spectrum is derived using irreducible unitary representations, and the corresponding Sturmian radial basis is obtained analytically. Furthermore, $\mathrm{SU}(1,1)$ coherent states are constructed and their time evolution is analyzed, revealing a characteristic radial breathing behavior. The results show that the Dunkl deformation introduces parity-dependent modifications in the spatial structure of the system while preserving its underlying algebraic dynamics.

bite.hook: Researchers solve the 2D Dunkl-Pauli equation for spin-1/2 particles using su(1,1) algebraic symmetry.
tldr: The team analyzed the Dunkl-Pauli equation for a spin-1/2 particle in a magnetic field using an algebraic approach.
They used Schrödinger factorization to identify the su(1,1) symmetry and derive the energy spectrum and radial basis.
The analysis reveals that Dunkl deformation alters the spatial structure of the system while keeping its algebraic dynamics intact.
bite.whyItMatters: Understanding the symmetry of quantum systems helps physicists predict how particles behave in complex fields. This algebraic approach simplifies solving difficult equations that describe how quantum particles move.
bite.eli5: Think of a quantum particle as a dancer. The Dunkl-Pauli equation describes the dance, and the magnetic field is the music. By finding the 'algebraic symmetry,' the researchers found the hidden rhythm of the dance, allowing them to predict exactly how the particle moves without having to track every single step.
